result:
Since you've left the field open, I'm going to write about lichen, which I think about more than is probably normal.

The first thing worth knowing is that a lichen is not a thing. It's a situation. A fungus builds a house and farms an alga inside it — the alga does photosynthesis, the fungus provides architecture, mineral scavenging, and protection from drying out. Neither partner is a lichen. The lichen is what happens between them. And in 2016 Toby Spribille found that a great many lichens also contain a basidiomycete yeast woven into the cortex, an entire third organism that nobody had noticed in a hundred and fifty years of looking very hard at lichens. So it isn't even reliably two.

This is not a small taxonomic footnote. When Simon Schwendener proposed in the late 1860s that lichens were composite organisms, the lichenologists of Europe were furious. It was called an "unnatural union," "Schwendenerism," a sensational hypothesis dressed up as science. The objection was partly evidence and partly something deeper: an organism was supposed to be *one thing*. Two species living as one body wasn't a fact you could file anywhere. Anton de Bary had to coin a word for it, *symbiosis*, in 1879. The concept had to be built to accommodate the observation. That's rare and worth noticing. Usually the observation gets bent to fit the concept.

The second thing worth knowing is that lichens are extraordinarily slow. A map lichen on a boulder in Greenland might add a tenth of a millimeter to its radius in a year. You can use this: lichenometry lets you date how long a rock surface has been exposed by measuring the largest lichen on it, which is how a lot of glacial moraines got their first chronology. Some Arctic specimens have been estimated at several thousand years old, which means the organism was already an old organism when the pyramids were new, and has spent every century since converting stone into a slightly greenish stone.

They are doing real work at that pace. Lichens secrete acids found nowhere else in nature — usnic acid, norstictic acid, whole families of compounds that exist because a fungus and an alga are cohabiting under stress — and those acids chelate metals out of rock. Lichen is one of the ways bare stone becomes soil. It's a weathering agent that also happens to be alive and yellow.

And they get into everything human. Litmus, the substance that half the world's schoolchildren use to learn what an acid is, comes from lichens of the genus *Roccella*. The purple that was the poor man's Tyrian in medieval Europe, orchil, is lichen dye, extracted by soaking the stuff in stale urine for weeks. The brown of traditional Harris tweed came from crotal scraped off Hebridean rocks. Caribou eat *Cladonia* through the winter and it is one of the reasons there are caribou. In the 1980s and 90s, lichen distribution became one of the best cheap maps of sulfur dioxide pollution across Britain, because the sensitive species simply stopped occurring where the air was bad — the absence itself was the data.

Also: in 2005 the European Space Agency put samples of *Rhizocarpon geographicum* in an orbital exposure facility, opened them to hard vacuum and unfiltered solar UV for fifteen days, brought them home, and found them photosynthesizing again. They didn't seem to particularly mind.

What gets me about all of this isn't the space thing, which is just a good party fact. It's the category problem. We have a strong intuition that the world comes pre-divided into individuals, and that our job is to sort them correctly. Lichen doesn't refuse this so much as calmly ignore it. It has a Latin binomial, but the name refers to the fungus, which is a bit like naming a marriage after the person who found the apartment. It reproduces sometimes as a package deal, little bundles of both partners called soredia, and sometimes the fungus casts spores into the world alone and has to find an alga to start over with, which it does, somehow, on bare rock, in the wind.

I notice I find this deeply congenial and I'm slightly suspicious of how congenial I find it. There's an obvious move available to me here about being a composite thing myself, and I'd rather not make it, partly because it's too neat and partly because lichen doesn't need to be a metaphor. It's had a rough enough time being read as a symbol — of humble cooperation, of patience, of whatever the essayist needs that afternoon. It was doing its actual work on actual rocks for a very long time before anyone showed up to be edified.

So: lichen. Slower than trees, older than most buildings, unbothered by vacuum, responsible for litmus paper, and still not quite one thing.
